newsitem.title: GERMANY: German govt names Scheuerle top telecoms watchdog.
newsitem.headline: German govt names Scheuerle top telecoms watchdog.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet on Wednesday appointed Klaus-Dieter Scheuerle, a senior post ministry official, to head a new watchdog agency for the telecoms sector after liberalistion on January 1, 1998.

Although widely expected, the choice is controversial because of criticism from the telecommunications industry that Scheuerle would not be tough enough in dealing with Deutsche Telekom, the incumbent phone monopoly.
German govt names Scheuerle top telecoms watchdog

The cabinet ignored the recommendation of the Regulatory Council, a temporary body made of up representatives of state governments and parliament, which had proposed appointing Peter Landsberg, former chairman of Alcatel SEL.
The new watchdog, the Regulatory Agency, will be under the wing of the economics ministry and begins operating on January 1, 1998, when the telecoms sector opens to full competition.

Scheuerle will head the new agency and he will have two deputies -- Arne Boernsen, the Social Democratic (SPD) chairman of parliament's postal affairs committee, and Volker Schlegel, economics department chief at the German Embassy in Washington.
German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said in a statement that the telecommunications market must be tapped for all of its growth potential.
"I will continue the path of liberalisation started by the Post and Telecommunications Ministry. These markets hold huge growth opportunities and potential innovation," he said.
Germany's Federation of Taxpayers has called the decision a classic example of cronyism and sharply criticised the size of the salaries the three officials would receive.
The Federal Accounting Office has also criticised the salaries, which are higher than at any other state agency.
As head of the agency, Scheuerle will receive a monthly salary of 18,535 marks ($10,600), while his deputies will each receive 14,573 marks.
Hans-Martin Bury, a SPD telecoms expert, told InfoRadio in Berlin, that choosing a civil servant to head the new agency was not the best solution.
He warned that the choice of Scheuerle could give the impression that the government was more interested in protecting the value of its 74 percent stake in Telekom than in ensuring fair competition.
